@@51357882 <h> Engineering Plants To Withstand Climate Change Challenges <p> For plants , climate change promises one thing for sure -- increased levels of stress . After all , plants put down roots . They do n't have the option of moving to where the weather suits them . Wider fluctuations in temperatures and increasing levels of aridity in many regions around the world are already making their lives more difficult . <p> Plants are highly complex and sensitive systems . Even in zones with stable climates today , variations in light levels can reduce growth rates and crop yields . For example , plants have developed sophisticated cellular mechanisms that protect them against the deleterious effects of high light intensities on photosynthesis . In one such photoprotective process , the excess light energy is dissipated as heat before it can damage the photosynthetic apparatus . This depresses yields but it is very much in the plant 's interest . <p> Three enzymes play a key role in this adaptation process , which are referred to as V , P and Z for short . In a paper published in 2016 , which drew a great deal of attention , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ proteins in tobacco plants , thus increasing the amounts of the enzymes produced in the leaves . They subsequently observed , under field conditions , that these ' VPZ ' lines grew faster rates than did control plants with normal levels of the enzymes . LMU biologists Antoni Garcia-Molina and Dario Leister have now performed essentially the same experiment in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana ( thale cress ) . <p> Their results confirm that , as in the case of tobacco , higher levels of V , P and Z reduce rates of photosynthesis while enabling the plants to adapt more rapidly ( in fact , even faster than tobacco ) to fluctuating light levels . Crucially however , the Arabidopsis VPZ lines did not grow faster than control plants . On the contrary , overexpression of the three enzymes resulted in retarded growth . " This clearly shows that it 's not quite as easy to produce plants that are better adapted as some research groups have confidently suggested , " Leister remarks . " In fact , higher levels of photoprotection may actually interfere with the operation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <p> For Leister , these data essentially demonstrate that targeted adaptation of plants to facilitate successful adjustment to changing climatic conditions is likely to be a very complicated task . They certainly show that one can not always expect to confer increased resistance to desiccation or optimize yields under fluctuating light levels simply by adjusting the levels of a few proteins . " The physiological processes in plants are tightly interconnected . This makes it impossible to predict the effects of flipping this switch or tightening that screw , " he says . <p> This explains why he and his colleagues approach the problem of targeted adaptation from the perspective of systems biology , which takes a " holistic " view , as he calls it . For example , efforts to increase the yield or biomass by increasing the efficiency of photosynthesis must also ensure that the extra energy available is in fact channeled into increased growth . In principle , enhanced photosynthetic performance should result in the capture of more energy and in higher levels of metabolites . But this extra energy and abundance of chemical compounds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ absence of any " added value " , increased rates of photosynthesis can prove to be detrimental to plants . <p> The analysis of complex relationships like this is the raison d ' ? tre of the Transregional Collaborative Research Center TR175 , of which Leister is the principal coordinator . The scientists involved in the project seek to understand how plants react to biotic and abiotic environmental factors , such as drought , light levels and temperature , by analyzing their impact on the concentrations of all measurable metabolites , transcripts and proteins in plant cells . With the help of these data , they hope to identify the key components that allow plants to cope with varying conditions . <p> In the case of crop plants that are indispensable for human nutrition , the mechanisms that underlie trade-offs between growth rates , increases in biomass and yields must also be taken into consideration . " In the context of climate change , the idea is to help plants to adapt to the changing conditions by introducing targeted genetic changes that allow them to handle the altered environmental parameters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as " assisted evolution " . " In order to have a realistic chance of finding sustainable solutions , we must adopt a systematic approach to the active adaptation of plants to the changing environmental conditions , " he says . <p> In this respect , some progress has already been made in certain species of algae that have very short generation times , which permits instances of successful adaptation to be rapidly detected . Such systems can then serve as sources of potentially useful genetic mutations that can be introduced into green plants . <h> RELATED ARTICLES <p> New work shows how using next-generation DNA sequencing on ancient packrat middens--nests made out of plant material , fragments of insects , bones , fecal matter , and urine--could provide ecological snapshots of Earth 's past . <p> Computational biologists at Carnegie Mellon University have taken an algorithm used to study social networks , such as Facebook communities , and adapted it to identify how DNA and proteins are interconnected into communities within the cell nucleus .

@@51359569 <p> Lawyers at Ecojustice plan to argue in front of the Supreme Court this week that environmental protection is an underlying principle of the Constitution , just like democracy , human rights and the rule of law . <p> The environmental law charity is one of many intervenors making arguments on Jan. 16 , in a hearing that will decide whether the B.C. government can block heavy oil from flowing through the expansion of the Trans Mountain pipeline . <p> But while the case has important ramifications for the fate of that fossil fuel project , Ecojustice 's approach has much more profound implications . <p> If the constitutional status of the environment is recognized , that could ensure its protection beyond the whims of the government of the day . In other words , like issues surrounding human rights , future governments could be constrained in what they could do to the environment . <p> " The Supreme Court has said over and over again that these sort of matters are so fundamental to our existence , to our society that , even though they 're not written explicitly in the Constitution , they still exist and they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ said Ecojustice staff lawyer Kegan Pepper-Smith , in an interview Jan. 15 in his Ottawa office . <p> " And we say , although environmental protection is n't written into the Constitution , it 's so fundamental that it should also be considered one of those principles . " <p> What 's more , Canada 's courts have often respected what 's known as the " living tree doctrine , " which says the Constitution must be reinterpreted as the times change and society evolves . <p> In a 1985 decision on Manitoba language rights , for instance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fundamental principle of the Canadian constitutional order . " <p> More famously , its 1998 decision on Quebec secession states that the Constitution " is more than a written text , " and in fact " a superficial reading of selected provisions of the written constitutional enactment , without more , may be misleading . " <p> The case on Thursday will hear the federal government defend its constitutional authority over transportation projects that cross provincial boundaries . " <p> From those first notes on the keyboard to the then-15-year-old 's angelic coo , " Baby " stepped out of the rock ' n ' roll-heavy Canadian musical landscape and began to build a bridge between the pop world and the rest of us , offering a much-needed reprieve from the default offering of mainstream-beloved dudes holding guitars and wearing plaid shirts . ( See : Arkells , The Sheepdogs . ) It was born from the relatively new world of YouTube stars ( of which Bieber was a pioneer ) , produced by industry heavyweights The-Dream and Tricky Stewart and performed alongside Ludacris . As the lead single off Bieber 's first full-length album , My World 2.0 , its lyrics were simple ( " Oh , for you , I would 've done whatever / And I just ca n't believe we ai n't together " ) , its melody was easy to sing along with and its catchiness made it an aggressive earworm that could quickly convince anybody listening that it was the greatest song in the world . Hell , even as a 2010s-era indie music snob , it only took a handful of listens for me to brand myself a Belieber and brag to anyone who would listen that Stratford , Ont. , was only about half an hour away from my hometown . ( Years later , I would sit on the Avon Theatre steps where Justin used to play his acoustic guitar and fight back the urge to tell anybody who passed me that he was my son . ) It was such an easy song to like . And ultimately , it was like a mainline to being young again . <p> Because that 's what made a song like " Baby " so easily digestible : where the magic of crushes and innocent heartbreak that accompany low-stakes relationships tend to fade the further into adulthood you go , Bieber 's premiere single served as a delightful time machine . It evoked emotions many of us had n't felt since junior high and tapped into a nostalgia that ended up defining the decade in its own way . It sounded like butterflies , the first time holding hands , and quiet but bold -- albeit still very harmless -- emotive declarations . It was a tiny boy singing about how much he liked someone and how much he hoped they could be together despite knowing it might never be so . It was the most fun . <p> As we know , not falling in love with the song proved impossible . It debuted at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and was the most-viewed video on YouTube until Psy 's " Gangnam Style " surpassed it in November of 2012 . True , the song -- and Bieber -- obviously followed the formula that pop music has long been built on ( a young star sings about puppy love as a means to launch a brand he 'll inevitably abandon in a handful of years as he grows up ) . But in 2010 , it felt brand new -- and newer still for Canada , a nation that 's global musical offerings at the time felt far removed from the majesty of a young pop singer who 'd used the internet to earn the attention of Usher and , subsequently , the audiences Usher had placed him in front of . It felt like a chance to relive the ' 90s and the young generation of pop stars it produced ( Britney Spears , *NSYNC , Backstreet Boys ) , but under an updated , improved Canadian lens . It felt like we could learn from old industry mistakes . It felt like a new era -- the dawn of a new day . <p> And it was so easy to sing and dance to , and as a result , easier still to defend to naysayers whose problems with the song seemed rooted in cynicism and bitterness . After all , " Baby " was a joy ! A source of light ! A dream come true ! It played proudly at parties , in cars and in our homes as we got ready , and then it morphed into what felt like an anthem for a decade , one that would become further defined by Canadian artists who were exciting and new and who made listening to their music feel like we were having the best time on Earth -- even when J-Biebs released a single called " Sorry . " <p> Anne T. Donahue is a writer , person and author of Nobody Cares : Essays , and her favourite song is Al Pacino 's " Dunkaccino " commercial . <p> Are we human , or are we Na'vi ? The decade begins auspiciously for French-language cinema -- and it 's only le tip de l'iceberg . <p> The 2010s saw screen industries worldwide experience a fundamental metamorphosis : streaming services changed the game in terms of the ways audiences watch content and how creators compete in the marketplace . But parallel to this momentous business-model transformation , Canadian films were busy solidifying their indisputable place in the arthouse world . Indigenous filmmakers also brought some of the most affecting stories to our screens ; a new wave of filmmakers revitalized the indie scene while veterans got called to work on some of the biggest series on Earth ; and gender parity became a serious priority with the #TimesUp and #MeToo movements . And on the world stage , after decades of sporadic success outside the province , Qu ? b ? cois filmmakers embarked on a stratospheric upward trajectory with a wild combo of arthouse and blockbuster gold . <p> It 's been exceptionally exciting to witness the international success of our Quebec filmmakers like Villeneuve and Vall ? e , who , in the last 10 years , have leapt from their acclaimed francophone work to helm major American studio projects like Prisoners , Dallas Buyers Club , Sicario and Wild . Villeneuve also dove into sci-fi with Arrival and Blade Runner 2049 , while Vall ? e went on to participate in giving television its current Golden Age status with Big Little Lies and Sharp Objects . Meanwhile , Dolan became mind-bogglingly prolific and had his arthouse blockbuster moment with Mommy , then produced Adele 's " Hello " music video and directed in Europe and the U.S. <p> As a francophone Qu ? b ? coise living in Toronto and working in the film industry , this decade felt like watching the kids we had cared for and supported emotionally and financially for years suddenly fly the coop and leave home . Off they went with their new beautiful-people families , while we stood in the window waving lovingly -- and slightly nervously . " How great to see our talented kids succeed ! ... Are they going to come back ? Should we cut their allowances ? Are they still OURS ? ' ' As some were hitting the Hollywood big-time , artists like Denis C ? t ? , Anne ? mond , S ? bastien Pilote , Mathieu Denis and Simon Lavoie were also becoming international festival darlings embraced by out-of-province and out-of-country audiences alike . <p> Discussing homegrown artists who break out internationally is always tricky . Patriotism and pride come into play , and inevitably , questions are raised around what it means to be Canadian and make Canadian content . ( The number of panel discussions and essays centred around the question " What makes Cancon Cancon ? " speaks to this . ) It 's trickier still when it comes to Quebec filmmakers . How can we explain their sweeping success and the resonance of their work ? <p> It 's my opinion that non-dominant cultures tend to be more observant -- and their cultural outputs often richer -- than dominant ones . In Canada , Qu ? b ? cois filmmakers have a fertile onscreen history of non-conformity , risk-taking and unabashedly high levels of emotions . It 's a thrill to see the common themes , patterns and interests of these artists emerge in their work -- to find the guiding tropes of love and living fully with the ones closest to you in Dolan 's work ; the fascination with existential mysteries on Earth and beyond in Villeneuve 's ; the exploration of personal differences and uneasy human reconciliations in Vall ? e 's ; and the deep humanism in Falardeau 's and Archambault 's . These can be observed from the filmmakers ' first features all the way to the largest American studio projects they 've worked on . They have successfully put their indomitable signature on each and every project . <p> To protect and promote its culture , Quebec projects have also , on average , been better funded and have gone through longer gestation periods than projects in the rest of the country . Many of these artists ' first and second features were noticed fast , and came at a time when world cinema and film festivals were more influential than they had ever been , right before the content boom we 're now experiencing . The rest of Canada is arguably more culturally open than Quebec ( I 'm looking at you , Bill 21 ) but has yet to truly tap into its multitude of storytelling options and voices . It takes time and money to develop writers and filmmakers , and it takes bold greenlighting decisions to birth projects that can cut through the noise . <p> As we approach the dawn of a new decade , I see the following future in my crystal ball/champagne flute : Canada is at the top of its onscreen game . Co-production treaties are activated left , right and centre . The list of overachievers that dominate pop culture , whose projects are seen by hundreds of thousands of audience members on a consistent basis , is five times as long -- and more varied . And it includes names like Elle-M ? ij ? Tailfeathers , Kathleen Hepburn , Jeff Barnaby , Albert Shin , Johnny Ma , Jasmin Mozaffari , Andrew Cividino , Stephen Dunn , Alethea Arnaquq-Baril , Matt Johnson and Kazik Radwanski ( to name just a few ) . Major projects are made with our money and also without -- and that 's OK , as Toronto and the rest of Canada welcome major productions , and our filmmakers shape them , here and elsewhere . <p> The Quebec success story of the 2010s teaches us that great artists are global in appeal , that we do n't need to fret over losing them ( or worry that they 'll lose their unique artistry and local values ) and that films and series that resonate with large audiences can play a significant role in cultural rapprochement and understanding . In a country as ethnically diverse as ours , we can use film and television to move away from our so-called cultural silos . We have the people , the talent and the perspectives we need to create the big , bold Cancon canon we 've all been waiting for . <p> Magali Simard is the City of Toronto 's Film Sector Development Officer and spent years as a Canadian and International film programmer at TIFF . <p> It 's fitting that one of C ? line Dion 's biggest songs is called " A New Day Has Come " because upon the debut of her second Las Vegas residency ( called Celine ) in 2011 , she sparked the Dion renaissance that only seems to be getting stronger even now . Here are 10 examples . <h> The Twilight Saga ( 2008 -- 2012 ) <p> In the late aughts , there was nothing hotter than vampire romance , and by 2010 , it was like someone had slashed an artery on the whole trend . True Blood , The Vampire Diaries : softbois with fangs were bloody everywhere -- and The Twilight Saga started the frenzy . Starring ( then ) real-life couple Kristen Stewart and Robert Pattinson , the franchise spun four books into five movies . Three of the five premiered in the 2010s : Eclipse and Breaking Dawn -- Part 1 and 2 . And all three of those were shot in B.C. -- largely in the Vancouver area , where fans were known to mob sets ( and sign up for location tours ) . Each annual instalment generated more international bank than the last . Never a critical hit , the series was a pop culture titan , bolstered by legions of " Twihards . " Stan culture came to dominate the decade , and the acolytes of this schlocky supernatural romance more or less signalled the first wave . <h> Scott Pilgrim vs. the World ( 2010 ) <p> Sometime around 2012 , the superhero genre swallowed the Infinity Gauntlet or something -- metastasising into an endless string of monster franchises , each farting million-dollar bills and licensing deals . But in a decade of mega-powered blockbusters , Scott Pilgrim was always going to be the misfit . The hero wears obscure band tees , not vibranium battle armour . And directed by Edgar Wright ( Hot Fuzz , Baby Driver ) , it 's a hyper-stylized rom-com blended with a few rounds of Street Fighter . Scott ( Michael Cera ) falls for Ramona ( Mary Elizabeth Winstead ) , but before they can go on a semi-normal date , he 'll have to K.O. her seven evil exes -- including , fun fact , the future Captain America ( Chris Evans ) . Acclaimed but never a smash , it 's the rarest of comic book adaptations : a movie that 's lovingly faithful to the source material . And those graphic novels , which make up a six-part series by Bryan Lee O'Malley , are a time capsule of 2000s Toronto . The same could be said of the movie , filmed at a time when indie rock ruled ( Broken Social Scene and Metric appear on the soundtrack ) , the Sonic Boom record store was still on Bloor Street and 20-something dirtbags shared basement apartments in the Annex . ( Actually , that last bit is still true . ) <p> ( Universal Pictures ) <h> Inception ( 2010 ) <p> When it comes to the top-grossing movies of the decade , there 's not much in the way of variety . You 've got your reboots , your action franchises and a bunch of G-rated Disney extravaganzas . But every now and then , there was still room for an original , standalone story to squeeze into blockbuster territory . And when movie-goers gambled on something fresh , they chose sci-fi -- dark and puzzling but still explosion-packed sci-fi , like Christopher Nolan 's Inception . A heist movie where the robbers break into dreams , Leonardo DiCaprio leads an all-star cast ( including Halifax 's Ellen Page ) . And while the subconscious-hopping takes the action to sets all over the world , from England to Morocco to Los Angeles , the movie 's big final action sequence -- a ski chase straight out of James Bond -- was shot in Alberta . The Fortress Mountain Resort in Kananaskis stands in for a snowy nightmare maze . <h> Interstellar ( 2014 ) <p> Writer/director Christopher Nolan hopped back to Alberta for his next sci-fi adventure . But since the story 's set in a near-future dystopia , spots including Nanton , Fort Macleod and Lethbridge got a dustbowl makeover . That scene where a " doozy " of a dirt cloud spoils a baseball game ? It 's arguably less memorable than all the stuff in space , but when else are the New York Yankees ever going to play in Okotoks ? The movie was the 10th highest grossing picture of the year , worldwide . <h> The Witch ( 2015 ) <p> Of all the instant classics this decade produced , horror movies were some of the best : Get Out , The Babadook , Crimson Peak . But starting with The Witch in 2015 , another trend emerged . Audiences had an appetite for a particular strain of high-concept terror . Cheap scares were out , swapped for a far more chilling brand of storytelling : slow-festering , existential despair . Think of Ari Aster 's Hereditary and Midsommar -- both , incidentally , produced by A24 , the same company that distributed The Witch . Writer-director Robert Eggers turned Kiosk , Ont. into the grey woods of 17th-century New England in this Canada/U.S. co-production . The period language is alien . The mood is claustrophobic -- appropriate , considering you 're trapped on a farm with family of Puritan zealots . And the supernatural mystery of the plot ultimately crescendos into a finale that 's pure horror and ecstasy all at once . <h> The Revenant ( 2015 ) <p> It 's Leonardo DiCaprio versus the wilderness -- the Canadian wilderness . Inspired by the true story of an 1820s frontiersman , The Revenant ultimately won DiCaprio his first acting Oscar and would claim best drama honours at the Golden Globes that same year . Producing the thing was a technical feat -- just a shade less tricky than wrestling a grizzly bear . With a few small exceptions , everything was shot in Alberta and B.C. , and to capture those Rocky Mountain vistas , cinematographer Emmanuel " Chivo " Lubezki used nothing but natural light . <p> ( IMBD ) <h> Fifty Shades trilogy ( 2015 -- 2018 ) <p> What started as NSFW Twilight fan fiction produced one of the highest-grossing R-rated film franchises ever . Go ahead and file that under " things that could only happen in the 2010s . " And like The Twilight Saga before it , Fifty Shades 's big-screen adaptations were made in Vancouver . Instead of Washington State University , na ? ve heroine Anastasia Steele hangs out on the University of British Columbia campus . ( The Ubyssey would 've totally spiked her Christian Grey profile . ) And Grey Enterprises ? It 's the Bentall 5 building downtown . Universally panned , just like the bestselling books that spawned it , Fifty Shades was nevertheless a phenomenon . ( Book Club , anyone ? ) Plus , where the movies only scored Razzies , their soundtracks were winners . " Earned It " by Toronto 's The Weeknd is one of the more notable cuts . Nominated for an Oscar , it clinched the Grammy for best R&amp;B performance . <h> Deadpool and Deadpool 2 ( 2016 , 2018 ) <p> Sure , sure ... you 've been following him since his days on The Odyssey . But Ryan Reynolds locked his superstar status on Deadpool . Love or loathe its smirking meta spin on superhero action , both the original and the 2018 sequel were total hits , ranking among the 10 highest grossing movies worldwide in their respective years . And they were both shot in Vancouver . In 2019 , the city 's tourism department even launched a contest . The prize : a trip to Reynolds 's hometown . For a city to latch on to a movie franchise like that -- a movie franchise that shut down the Georgia Viaduct for two weeks ... that 's got to say something about its mass appeal . Other notable filming locations include Chinatown and Gastown . ( The winner of the contest , by the way , got the chance to visit both spots on a special Deadpool tour . ) <h> It and It Chapter Two ( 2017 , 2019 ) <p> Because the world was n't horrible enough in 2017 , It came back . The story of a child-murdering clown alien , it 's one of Stephen King 's best-known creations , but this particular adaptation -- which shot several scenes in and around Toronto -- is now the highest grossing horror movie ever made . The Toronto mansion used for some of the " It House " interiors is now a bit of a local tourist attraction . ( Float on down to 450 Pape Avenue if you dare to see it in person . ) <p> ( Brooke Palmer/Warner Bros ) <h> The Shape of Water ( 2017 ) <p> A year into the Trump presidency , as pop culture was increasingly reflecting the social #issues of the moment , Guillermo del Toro 's The Shape of Water told a story just as critical of the world 's various injustices and systemic ickiness -- but it served it up as a Cold War fairy tale . Winner of best picture at the 90th Academy Awards , it was also the most-nominated film of the year . A trio of Canadian production designers walked away with Oscars , too , and Toronto notably features in the film . ( Hawkins 's character lives above a gilded cinema -- the real-life Elgin Theatre , where The Shape of Water screened at TIFF . ) <p> Considering the vastness of YouTube , it was a small miracle that the Ben Shirinian -- directed short film " Lost In Motion " earned millions of views and went on to spark hope in anyone working in the arts that there 's life in digital distribution . Admittedly , despite the attention given to Guillaume C ? t ? -- the choreographer and principal dancer of the National Ballet of Canada who also starred in the film -- " Lost in Motion " did n't change the distribution game . But it 's exciting that even in the era of viral videos , the audience went wild for dance , for classical music and for a corner of the arts world that , unfairly , gets so overlooked . <p> The sixth novel written by the late Ojibway writer Richard Wagamese , Indian Horse was released in January and garnered overwhelming acclaim for its heart-wrenching depiction of Canada 's residential school system and the egregious abuses suffered by students . Taking place over the course of 30 years , the story follows a young man named Saul Indian Horse who makes his way into the hockey world and , after a series of racist attacks , confronts his traumatizing history . The book earned Wagamese the inaugural Burt Award for First Nations , Inuit and M ? t is Young Adult Literature ( then known as the Burt Award for First Nations , M ? t is and Inuit Literature ) , and in 2017 , the film adaptation premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival ( TIFF ) . Crushingly , Richard Wagamese passed away in March of that year . <p> When Montreal-based director Emily Kai Bock joined forces with Grimes ( born Claire Boucher ) and cinematographer Evan Prosofsky for the video for " Oblivion , " the trio likely had no idea that their limited budget and simple premise would garner 200,000 views in just a few days . But how could it not ? Shot among a 50,000-person crowd of motorbike rally spectators in a football stadium ( and a mosh pit made up of Boucher 's brother and his friends ) , the video juxtaposed the tiny Boucher atop the shouting , shoving , shirtless masses and created a playful effect that also addressed themes of traditional masculinity . It also helped launch her into the art-pop stratosphere from which she has yet to return . ( Come back to us , Claire . ) <p> Four years after first forming , the Ottawa-based A Tribe Called Red made their full-length debut with the release of their self-titled album , which went on to be longlisted for the Polaris Music Prize . Originally consisting of DJs Ehren " Bear Witness " Thomas of the Cayuga First Nation , Ian " DJ NDN " Campeau of the Nippising First Nation and Dan " DJ Shub " General , Mohawk of the Six Nations Grand River ( though General was replaced by Tim " 2oolman " Hill , Mohawk of the Six Nations Grand River , in 2014 and Campeau left in 2017 ) , the electronic music group drew much-deserved attention for their mix of hip hop , dance and reggae alongside remixes of traditional powwow songs . Following this , they launched their first world tour , released two more albums and three EPs , and took home the award for group of the year at the 2018 Juno Awards . ( So do n't ever let anyone tell you Canadian music is exclusively indie rock or dudes in plaid . ) <p> On April 16 -- just weeks after his 17th birthday -- Calgary-bred pianist Jan Lisiecki released his album of Mozart concertos as a debut for the label Deutsche Grammophon . It featured Mozart 's Piano Concerto No. 20 and No. 21 , and was quickly declared a " triumph . " It was ( and is ) also a further testament to why none of us should 've been allowed to quit piano lessons as a kid . <p> In a moment that was highly deserved and long overdue , Obsidian Theatre -- Canada 's leading Black theatre company -- stunned at the Dora Mavor Moore Awards in June when it conquered the play and musical theatre categories simultaneously . Suzan-Lori Parks 's Topdog/Underdog even beat out War Horse ( remember War Horse ? ! ) when it was named the year 's outstanding production of a play , while Caroline , or Change earned the prize for outstanding production of a musical . Originally founded in 2000 , the Obsidian Theatre continues to elevate Black artists in Canada . ( If you 're in Toronto , be sure to take in something from their current program ) . <p> In July of 2012 , we all set out on a journey : after four seasons of action , adventure , the Albuquerque underworld and Heisenberg , Breaking Bad 's fifth and last season premiered -- and brought with it an intensity I ca n't possibly describe in a simple paragraph . ( It was so intense , as you remember , that it was split into two sub-seasons and officially wrapped in the fall of 2013 . ) But of course , the series 's rare brand of genius and grit was thanks in part to Canadians Michelle MacLaren , who directed 11 episodes and served as an executive producer , and Moira Walley-Beckett , who worked on the show as both a writer and producer and earned an Emmy for outstanding writing after she penned the episode " Ozymandias . " They are the danger . <p> I like sci-fi -- mostly the quiet kind , where people are stuck in space alone with maybe one book or maybe zero books . Silence that ranges from contemplative to evoking sheer terror is kind of my jam . So the work of Vancouver-based artist Kelly Richardson has always spoken to me . In particular , her Mariner 9 of 2012 -- a panoramic video installation that imagines a Mars of the future explored by an unmanned vehicle -- feeds my desire for bleak visions of faraway planets . Richardson sets her video on Mars during a dust storm among detritus from previous explorations of the planet . It suggests a future where the probes have outlived us -- as the artist puts it , where " several of the spacecraft continue to partially function , to do their intended jobs , to ultimately find signs of life whilst transmitting the data back to a planet where no one is left to receive it . " But there 's also hope in Richardson 's installations , most recently her Embers and the Giants , which memorializes an endangered old-growth forest in British Columbia and invites us to protect our landscape . <h> by Lise Hosein <h> by Tranna Wintour <p> The 2010s have been all about fame -- often vapid , toxic , shallow and undeserved fame , a new kind of parasitic stardom that almost anyone can attain just as long as they 're desperate enough . The decade started with the birth of Instagram and the rise of Keeping Up with the Kardashians , and it has ended with the word " influencer " worming its way into the Merriam-Webster dictionary . <p> Is n't it ironic , then , that one of Canada 's biggest superstars has spent this fame-monster decade being mostly invisible ? Alanis Nadine Morissette , where have you been ? <p> So how can I argue that Alanis matters as much now , at the end of this decade , as she did in the ' 90s ? Here 's one reason : her silence is golden . In a decade defined by the relentless noise of " content creation " and everyone doing everything they can to get likes and followers , silence is rare and precious . <p> Back in 1998 , Alanis gave us a song called " That I Would Be Good , " which became a mantra . " That I would be good even if I did nothing , " she sang . And this decade , she actually proved it . She 's proved that it is possible to disconnect from greed , the need for validation and the harmful idea that our worth is based on our productivity . She 's proved , by example , that we are all good and worthy and valuable even if we do less . And in this age of trying too hard , billionaire greed , late capitalism and its contribution to environmental crisis , what message could be more important than that ? <p> Here are nine other reasons why Alanis still matters : <h> She gave us Havoc and Bright Lights <p> In the last 10 years , Alanis Morissette has only released one studio album : 2012 's Havoc and Bright Lights . The album went largely overlooked but contained some true gems , including " Empathy , " " Receive " and " Havoc , " which I would argue are among her best songs . The album 's unheard call for empathy and mindfulness are also exactly what we need as we embark on a new decade -- one that will hopefully bring us closer to spiritual unity than this extremely divisive , destructive one has . <h> Jagged Little Pill is as relevant as ever ... <p> And nothing anyone at Jezebel can say will ever diminish the cultural significance and magnitude of this album . The mere fact that someone was able to light the internet on fire in 2019 by writing a review of a record that 's almost 25 years old tells you just how powerful this album is . In the last 10 years , Beyonc ? and Taylor Swift -- two of the biggest pop stars of the decade -- both performed covers of " You Ought a Know . " And in 2015 , Alanis herself released a beautiful 20th anniversary edition of the album , including never-before-heard demos. <h> ... and she 's turned it into a Broadway musical ! <p> At the tail-end of this decade , right when we need it most , Alanis has turned Jagged Little Pill into a musical with a book written by Diablo Cody . The show 's previews have received rave reviews , and it 's shaping up to be a Broadway smash . Alanis has also written two brilliant new songs for the musical : " Smiling " and " Predator . " <p> ( Daniel Zuchnik/Getty Images ) <h> She 's become an outspoken advocate for postpartum depression awareness <p> This decade , Alanis gave birth to her three children , Ever , Onyx and Winter ( a.k.a. the three luckiest kids in the world ) . With each birth , Alanis experienced postpartum depression ( PPD ) -- and over the course of these 10 years , she has never shied away from publicly sharing those experiences and what she 's learned in the hopes of helping other people in the same situation . Shortly after the birth of Winter this year , Alanis posted a raw and honest blog on her website , in which she described PPD as a " sneaky monkey with a machete -- working its way through my psyche . " <h> She started #MeToo <p> OK , that 's not exactly true . But the #MeToo movement has made me re-contextualize one of Alanis 's bigger hits , which I now ca n't help but see as a precursor to the movement . Released in 2002 , " Hands Clean " is Alanis 's account and calling out of sexual abuse and manipulation by a music industry figure she was working with in her early pop days -- and the lyrics still resonate . This summer , I did a show called Dear Alanis , where I performed a stripped-down piano version of the song ; I had never realized how devastating the lyric " Just make sure you do n't tell on me , especially to members of your family " was until I sung it myself . <h> She is transparent and radically vulnerable <p> For her entire career , she 's been accused of being juvenile and psychobabble-y in her writing , but it 's what makes her great . Her ability to share so transparently and vulnerably about self-worth , confidence and self-image in our current culture -- one that 's so obsessed with supposed perfection -- is revolutionary . <h> She started a self care-themed podcast <p> Alanis has done a lot of therapy , not only for her own benefit but for ours as well ! On Conversation with Alanis Morissette , she gives us access to some of the greatest minds in the worlds of wellness , healing and recovery . <h> She 's telepathic <p> Can Alanis hear me ? As I write this , Alanis has just announced the details of her new single and album ! I , along with all of her truest fans , have been waiting seven years for this moment . The album is titled the most Alanis-y title possible : Such Pretty Forks in the Road . I can not think of a better way to end this decade than with the promise of her musical return . <h> She is giving us a big reason to look forward to 2020 <p> In addition to announcing her new album , Alanis kicked off the final month of this decade by giving us all second offering of what does n't always come easy these days : excitement for the future . On Dec. 2 , 2019 , she announced that she would go on a 31-date ( though unfortunately only one of those is in Canada ) tour in 2020 to celebrate Jagged Little Pill 's 25th anniversary . How lucky are we to be entering our fourth decade in knowing Alanis ? <p> Tranna Wintour is a comedian , singer , writer and the co-host of Chosen Family on CBC Podcasts. <h> by Chandler Levack <p> Looking back on the 2010s , I 'm struck by the sweeping changes that impacted me , a Canadian female filmmaker , and my people . Attention turned to filmmakers like Cape Breton Island , N.S. 's Ashley McKenzie , compared to Robert Bresson by The New Yorker 's Richard Brody ; Toronto writer-director Stella Meghie , who was nominated for an Independent Spirit Award in 2017 for the screenplay for her first feature Jean of the Joneses ; filmmaker Joyce Wong , who took over a strip mall in Toronto 's North York area in Wexford Plaza , a film that could arguably be called the mumblecore answer to Rashomon ; dramatic-comedy filmmaker Molly McGlynn , Canada 's answer to Nicole Holofcener ; hybrid docudrama artist Heather Young , who won the FIPRESCI Prize for her first feature , Murmur , this year ; and discursive documentary rock star Sofia Bohdanowicz , whose lovely collaborations with actor/filmmaker Deragh Campbell deserve their own miniature chapbook . <p> While the #MeToo movement served as a dramatic trigger in the latter portion of the 2010s , highlighting the desperate need women have to tell our own stories , the entire decade was an embarrassment of riches in terms of high-quality work made by Canadian women . With Falls Around Her , Darlene Naponse gave Tantoo Cardinal her first starring role in her more than 40-year-long career , which has included over 120 film and television credits . But the 2010s truly belonged to Alanis Obomsawin , who at age 87 continues to produce films in partnership with the NFB . This decade alone , she produced six feature-long documentaries and a short film -- serving as a powerful inspiration for Canadian women to keep going , even when it feels like the hardest thing in the world . <p> After decades of being shut out by a male-dominated industry as the subjects of institutional sexism , the 2010s saw Canadian women finally being given the opportunity to fulfill their potential . As we enter the 2020s , one can only hope the best is yet to come . We met on the set of my very first acting job -- a film whose title I 'll omit to spare us both the embarrassment -- and we played boyfriend and girlfriend . Tat was sweet . She was polite . She did n't take up a lot of space . Not a child actor , not yet a woman , she was a model of Canadian kindness and patience . A few examples : <p> When I excitedly played her Hilary and Haylie Duff 's cover of " Material Girl " in my trailer , she smiled , nodded and pretended like she thought it was great . ( As a gay man , I stand by the fact that it objectively is . ) <p> When our director asked us to romantically " nuzzle noses " in a party scene , which we both felt was awkward and unnatural ( I mean , what teenagers do that -- let alone in public , surrounded by their parents and their parents ' friends ? ) , she went for it with me . Of course , being the obedient little 20-year-olds we were , not only did we do it , we head-butted each other on the first take and then profusely apologized . <p> When one actor paraded around bare-assed ( boxers pulled up into his butt crack for comedic effect ) between takes of Tat 's big crying scene , she -- like any great Canadian artist , pre-2010 -- took her bottled-up biliousness and put it into the work , delivering a performance ( real tears ! ) that , frankly , belonged in a much better movie . <p> The next time Tat and I were together on set was 10 years later , when I directed her in a short film I wrote called Apart From Everything . I was immediately struck by her confidence on set -- how she took the space she needed to do her work in a firm but friendly way . Any ideas I had about how our relationship might affect the work -- that she might be a pushover or do whatever I told her , just because we 're friends -- were unfounded . Because Tat is , first and foremost , a defender of the truth . So if I asked her to do something that felt unnatural or dishonest ( like , say , " nose nuzzling " ) , I had to justify why I needed it -- and more often than not , I realized that I did n't . She pushed and challenged me to be a smarter , more economical filmmaker in the most caring , collaborative way . <p> So what happened to Tat in that decade between sets ? How did this dutiful Regina girl stop apologizing so much and become the force that she still is today ? Well , obviously , she experienced a lot of personal growth , but also : Orphan Black ran for five seasons , winning her four consecutive Canadian Screen Awards for her performances . She acted opposite Jake Gyllenhaal and Dane DeHaan , and was dubbed " The Millennial Meryl Streep . " And ultimately , the quality ( and quantity ) of her work on Orphan Black -- boosted by the support of critics and Clone Clubbers alike -- won her an Emmy in 2016 , making her the first Canadian actor in a Canadian series ever to win an Emmy in a major dramatic category . <p> Looking back , I realize that regardless of the set , if there 's one time Tat has never said " sorry , " it 's between " action " and " cut . " She 's always been a fucking savage in the work itself , from her raw performance in 2010 's Grown Up Movie Star to beating the shit out of Nicole Kidman in last year 's Destroyer . ( The fact that that scene is n't already gay canon is , to me , a greater outrage than any Emmy snub . ) <p> The truth about not only Tat , but also Dan Levy ( the visionary co-creator of Schitt 's Creek and also a longtime friend ) and other Canadian artists , is that we 've always had the talent -- just maybe not the audacity to make it known . In the 2010s , it is n't that we earned the right to voice our opinion , stand up for our work and stop saying " sorry " -- it 's that we realized we 'd had that right all along . It 's a trend I hope continues in the 2020s : less obedience , less compromise , more empowerment , more ambition . Because regardless of whether the Emmys take notice , it 's going to make great TV . <p> Ben Lewis is an actor/writer/director from Toronto , best known for his role on the hit CW series Arrow . <p> There 's only one instance where it 's OK to bust out an acoustic guitar to sing the cover of a world-renowned song , and that 's if your name is Chris Hadfield and you are aboard the International Space Station , floating in zero gravity . After posting his efforts on YouTube , the astronaut 's version of David Bowie 's " Space Oddity " became the first music video ever performed in space and has since earned over 44.6 million views . Despite some legal issues stemming from the track 's publishing rights , it even earned the love of David Bowie himself , who took to Facebook and said it was " possibly the most poignant version of the song ever created . " In related news , I miss David Bowie . ( In unrelated news , space seems terrifying . ) <p> Canada 's institutions tokenized , ignored or exoticized Indigenous art for a really long time . That 's an old story . What is more heartening is their relatively recent acknowledgment of the role Indigenous art has played and continues to play in historical and contemporary culture . When it opened at the National Gallery of Canada in 2013 , Sakah ? n : International Indigenous Art was billed as offering the " largest-ever global survey of contemporary Indigenous art " and included work from Rebecca Belmore , Brian Jungen and the now late Annie Pootoogook , as well as artists from other regions like Finland , India and New Zealand . The exhibition was a moment to talk about identity and the impact and trauma of colonialism while celebrating the artists featured , a number of whom made work specifically for the show . ( Six years later , the National Gallery saw its largest-ever opening crowd for Sakah ? n 's followup , ? badakone. ) <h> by Lise Hosein <p> Starring Canadian besties Seth Rogen and Jay Baruchel , This Is the End -- a Rogen/Evan Goldberg -- **25;1548;TOOLONG joint -- took the terror and hilarity of the apocalypse to new heights with their version of what might happen when the world finally ends . It 's a parody of reality TV , a docu-drama about seeking human connection , a satire of capitalism and the inherent moral relativism it brews . And yeah , it 's also why you LOL 'd at a tweet about " Dumb Starbucks " at some point in 2014 . <p> And there 's something extremely 2010s about all of it . First of all , that concept . Once upon a time , your boomer aunt was n't obsessed with building her " personal brand " on Instagram -- but social media 's defined the decade , and as a result , we 've all learned to sell ourselves ( or at least feel very worried if we are n't ) . Marketing tactics have infiltrated ordinary life in ways that are increasingly absurd , and every time a NFY stunt went viral , it was like the universe clicking the " like button , " as if to say , yes , nothing you were taught makes sense anymore . <p> It 's our topsy-turvy reality that makes any given episode of NFY more confoundingly hilarious . A terrible business plan -- a literal joke -- can draw international publicity . Whose advice can you believe ? What can you believe , period ? What motivates people to believe the most obvious , calculated lie , despite all evidence to the contrary ? That 's the bigger , think-ier and way more 2010s question that underpins the whole series . <p> " Post-truth " might have a political whiff to it , but few terms define the decade quite like it . And rewatching NFY , nothing 's more important or flexible than Nathan 's understanding of the T-word . If a tactic bombs , he 'll call it a success -- or hire an actress who 'll tell him she loved it . <p> ( Comedy Central ) <p> On NFY , truth is a lie you have the confidence to believe . ( And according to Episode 1 , Nathan believes he has a ton of confidence . ) As a viewer , it becomes increasingly hard to keep the facts straight . Is NFY spoofing reality TV ? Or is it reality TV -- a show about a lonely comedian from Vancouver who happened to go to business school ? <p> Whatever the answer , if the 2010s have been a time of all-purpose confusion , few shows have nailed the decade quite like this one , and these are just 10 of its finest moments . <h> Petting Zoo ( S1 , E2 ) <p> The plan : Attract visitors to a petting zoo with a " hero pig . " <p> Follow every pedantic rule in the social media playbook , and there 's still no formula for going viral . The whole endeavour is inherently absurd , made even more bonkers if the gambit actually works . And in the fall of 2012 , NFY ( accidentally ? ) pulled it off when a YouTube video called " Pig rescues baby goat " became an international sensation . <p> If NFY has a fourth wall , this was the first scam to smash it . Later stunts , like Summit Ice -- " the world 's first outdoor apparel company to openly promote the true story of the holocaust " -- might have had a more positive real-world outcome . ( Fielder famously donated $150,000 of the profits to the Vancouver Holocaust Education Centre -- 150,000 U.S. dollars . ) But just two episodes into the series , the Petting Zoo bit proved the brilliance of NFY 's marketing satire . As for that YouTube video , it has more than 10 million views as of writing , and however it was made , it remains , per the description , " simply amazing . " <h> Gas Station ( S1 , E4 ) <p> The plan : Attract customers with cheap gas by offering a " completely legal rebate that absolutely no one claims . " <p> There 's barely an episode where Nathan is n't putting himself out there , trying to turn an awkward encounter with a client ( or an actor he found on Craigslist ) into something more . He might not say it out loud , but the character 's real KPI is friendship , and what , besides money , is a bigger motivation than the power of love ? <p> The series is packed with moments of human connection that are as unexpected as they are genuine . ( At least , they sure seem genuine . ) And one of the greatest examples happens on top of a mountain , where a vanload of people -- desperate for as little as a $10.91 rebate -- subject themselves to a six-hour hike , an overnight camping trip and Nathan 's endless riddles . Beyond a few supremely bizarre moments ( three words : naturopathic piss drinking ) , a fireside convo brings the group together and as Nathan says at the conclusion : " By the end of the night , I felt like I had made new friends . That 's where " The Hunk " cracks the show open . <p> If NFY 's the story of one man 's quest for attention -- and the lies he 'd tell to get it -- then it 's basically just The Bachelor . And in a thoroughly meta epiphany , Nathan discovers the effect his TV cameras have on people . Read : they 're friendly ! So , he invents a Bachelor-style reality show . ( He 's the handsome star . Back off , Tony Napoli . ) But after basking in the attention of 10 women hired off Craigslist , Nathan calls off the ruse . " I felt confident in myself knowing that if I ever wanted to find love , I could just create a fake reality show all over again . " <h> Realtor ( S2 , E1 ) <p> The plan : Reach an untapped market : " the 50 per cent of people who believe in ghosts . " <p> Ghosts ? They do n't exist . And putting aside quacks like Egon Spengler , the science is on my side . But belief 's a powerful thing . I suppose it 's what makes this segment one of the more powerful moments in NFY 's run : it 's just candid enough to shake your grasp of what 's genuine or scripted , fact or fiction . <p> First , though , some backstory . " Though delighted by her spooky new bench ads , Sue seems skeptical at first . But on Nathan 's advice , she teams up with a psychic , and on a routine home inspection , the guy claims to sense a malevolent presence . It 's an " incubus " -- which is way less surprising than Sue 's reaction . She was choked , she says . By a ghost . In Switzerland . And by the time they recruit an exorcist ( out , out , incubus ! ) things get even more real -- at least for Sue , who experiences an emotional breakdown while the exorcist does his thing . <h> Dumb Starbucks ( S2 , E5 ) <p> The plan : Get brand recognition by turning an indie cafe into the world 's first parody Starbucks . <p> Where there 's a loophole , there 's a way . These butt-covering details can turn a Byzantine act of deception into a Byzantine act of deception that 's legal -- and over four seasons of semantic manipulation , Dumb Starbucks remains NFY 's most celebrated moment . <p> A look-alike Starbucks that technically spoofs the world 's biggest coffee brand , Nathan cites " parody law " as his defense , and in 24 hours , the world was talking about the mysterious stunt . ( Could it be Banksy ? ) In the episode , Nathan reveals his involvement at a press conference , and it 's the happiest he 's ever been : " My business was not only a bona fide success , but for the first time in my life it felt like people actually wanted to be around me . Whatever I had done resonated with the entire world and the attention was like sunlight on my soul . " <h> The Movement ( S3 , E3 ) <p> The plan : " Turn the job of moving into America 's next fitness craze . " <p> The best weight loss systems usually have a " charismatic " fitness guru behind the brand , so Nathan hires a random bodybuilder named Jack to play the part , booking him a slew of TV appearances . As wellness fads go , The Movement 's not overtly sketchy , which might account for its success in the real world . There are no jade eggs involved , no sauna suits -- just a workout plan entirely focused on hauling boxes and furniture . And while the client ( a moving company ) was ultimately reluctant to use Nathan 's idea , the book he published for the episode -- The Movement : How I Got This Body by Never Going to the Gym in My Life -- was an Amazon bestseller . Were people interested in exercise tips or Jack 's tales of " jungle children " ? Like so many NFY mysteries , we may never know . <h> Smokers Allowed ( S3 , E5 ) <p> The plan : Become the " only drinking hole in town where people could legally smoke . " <p> Few things can push the limits of credulity like an artistic statement , and in this episode , Nathan exploits a loophole in California 's smoking laws , staging a " theatrical production " in a Pasadena tavern . By creating an " audience section " for the bar , the rest of the patrons will become de facto performers in his " slice of life " show ... Smokers Allowed . Because the idea is n't bonkers enough , the first audience loves it . ( Raves one woman after the show : " It 's so nothing in a way , but incredibly profound . It reminded me of Sam Shepard . " ) From there , Nathan 's game plan explodes . " You can make good money having people smoke here , " he tells the owner . " But you could make millions with a hit play . " And because this is NFY , he scours footage of the first " performance " to duplicate the experience , hiring actors to " embody the exact essence " of the original patrons . <h> The Hero ( S3 , E8 ) <p> The plan : Find an ordinary guy and transform him " into a national hero . " <p> There 's nobody quite like Nathan ( and the show 's cringiest scenes prove it ) . But he is , nevertheless , an imposter playing an imposter : a comedian posing as a business consultant ... posing as whatever suits his plan . <p> For the Season 3 finale , NFY takes that swindle to the extreme , with Nathan orchestrating a high-wire spectacle . If it 's successful , he 'll make a hero out of a stranger : a random dude ( Corey Calderwood ) who lets Nathan assume his identity -- and , you know , carry out the plot . Nathan enjoys playing Corey a little too much , and amazingly , the gambit succeeds . As promised , he inspires the public with a " death-defying tightrope walk for charity . " <h> The Anecdote ( S4 , E4 ) <p> The plan : Construct the " ultimate talk show anecdote . " <p> By the show 's final season , it was n't just ignoring the line between the NFY universe and our own -- it was erasing it entirely . Comedy Central wants him to promote the new season , he explains , but unlike other celebrities , he does n't have a wild and fabulous story to share . The solution : spend " nearly six hours " analyzing late-night interviews and write the perfect story . Then , spend $350,000 staging every detail so that everything happened to him " for real . " Few episodes push the definition of truth quite like this one . As for that talk show appearance , it killed . <h> Finding Frances ( S4 , E7 ) <p> NFY was always more than a prank show , but in four seasons , it had evolved from poo jokes to this : a feature-length movie ( documentary ? ) about love and the lies we tell ourselves . <p> The star is Bill Heath , a " Bill Gates impersonator " who first appears in Season 2 . Bill 's a recurring presence on the show , popping up in scams or even just visual gags , usually rambling about Microsoft and providing a little surreal colour . He 's 78 and lives alone . He 's never married . And according to Nathan , he regularly visits the production office where he 'll wind up sharing stories about Frances , a woman he has n't seen in more than 50 years . <p> In the style of a documentary mystery , the movie 's a search for Bill 's long-lost love . He 's convinced he 'll reach a happy ending , erasing a lifetime of misery . It 's an obvious delusion , but a romantic one -- the sort of beautiful lie you can build a story on . ( In Season 2 , there 's a blip of a visual gag where Nathan 's seen writing a " passion project " called Looking For Susan . I doubt it 's a coincidence . Are you ready to hear the truth that needs to be told ? " <p> These words became iconic the moment they were spoken by Wolastoqiyik musicologist , vocalist and composer Jeremy Dutcher . He was accepting the 2018 Polaris Music Prize for his debut album Wolastoqiyik Lintuwakonawa , sung entirely in the Wolastoq language -- a language that is severely endangered due to Canada 's policies of Indigenous assimilation and cultural genocide . His win marked the fourth Polaris Prize win by an Indigenous artist in five years , following Lido Pimienta , Buffy Sainte-Marie and Tanya Tagaq . This coincided with Indigenous artists dominating both literature and visual art awards : the Sobey Art Award has been awarded to three Indigenous artists since 2013 , and the Griffin Poetry Prize had three consecutive Indigenous winners from 2016 to 2018 . This year , Gwen Benaway became not only the first trans woman but also the first Indigenous trans woman to win a Governor General 's Literary Award . Since I wrote a piece examining the Indigenous renaissance Dutcher identified , even more Indigenous artists have been given the national attention they deserve . <p> While it would be romantic to say that all of these brilliant Indigenous artists coincidentally emerged in the art scene at the same time -- and that Canadians and Canadian arts institutions just so happened to recognize that brilliance at the same time -- it would n't exactly be accurate . The reality is that , despite the success of Indigenous artists prior to 2015 , there was n't a national push to both recognize and , more importantly , fund Indigenous artists until the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada ( TRC ) released its final report in December of that year . The TRC 's final report -- titled " Honouring the Truth , Reconciling for the Future " -- marked not only the birth of " reconciliation " as a political catchphrase , but also a cultural shift in how Indigenous art and artists were perceived and engaged with . <p> " You are in the midst of an Indigenous renaissance . Are you ready to hear the truth that needs to be told ? " <p> These words became iconic the moment they were spoken by Wolastoqiyik musicologist , vocalist and composer Jeremy Dutcher . He was accepting the 2018 Polaris Music Prize for his debut album Wolastoqiyik Lintuwakonawa , sung entirely in the Wolastoq language -- a language that is severely endangered due to Canada 's policies of Indigenous assimilation and cultural genocide . His win marked the fourth Polaris Prize win by an Indigenous artist in five years , following Lido Pimienta , Buffy Sainte-Marie and Tanya Tagaq . This coincided with Indigenous artists dominating both literature and visual art awards : the Sobey Art Award has been awarded to three Indigenous artists since 2013 , and the Griffin Poetry Prize had three consecutive Indigenous winners from 2016 to 2018 . This year , Gwen Benaway became not only the first trans woman but also the first Indigenous trans woman to win a Governor General 's Literary Award . Since I wrote a piece examining the Indigenous renaissance Dutcher identified , even more Indigenous artists have been given the national attention they deserve . <p> While it would be romantic to say that all of these brilliant Indigenous artists coincidentally emerged in the art scene at the same time -- and that Canadians and Canadian arts institutions just so happened to recognize that brilliance at the same time -- it would n't exactly be accurate . The reality is that , despite the success of Indigenous artists prior to 2015 , there was n't a national push to both recognize and , more importantly , fund Indigenous artists until the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada ( TRC ) released its final report in December of that year . The TRC 's final report -- titled " Honouring the Truth , Reconciling for the Future " -- marked not only the birth of " reconciliation " as a political catchphrase , but also a cultural shift in how Indigenous art and artists were perceived and engaged with . <p> Indigenous artists have always created incredible work , from the blankets Salish weavers constructed from goat hair and woolly dog hair to the intricate carvings made by Inuit sculptors from bones and antlers to Haudenosaunee raised beadwork . Unfortunately , because these works did n't fit colonial ideas of what constituted " art , " they were labeled either " crafts " or anthropological artifacts for centuries -- not art worthy of examining , studying and displaying in art museums . This extended to the literary realm as well . In her seminal book Survival : A Thematic Guide to Canadian Literature , Margaret Atwood theorized that the central symbol in Canada , and therefore Canadian literature , was survival . This was based on early settlers ' experiences of " bare survival in the face of ' hostile ' elements and/or Natives . " Though they did exist , Indigenous writers were not considered ; we only ever appear in the book as " hostile Natives " that white Canadians must survive . <p> In her pivotal 1991 paper " The Politics of Inclusion and Exclusion : Contemporary Native Art and Public Art Museums in Canada , " Mohawk curator Lee-Ann Martin named the ultimate effect of this erasure : " The exclusion of the arts of Native peoples implies that the artistic and cultural contributions to Canadian history by Canada 's First Nations Inuit , and M ? t is are non-existent . " Because our art and literature were not acknowledged , as far as the Canadian public was concerned , it did n't exist . And since Indigenous peoples ' supposed lack of history , art , politics , science , medicine and culture was often used to excuse Canada 's systematic attempts to wipe out our nations , this sort of erasure had concrete effects on our lives . <p> This colonial mentality -- that Indigenous people are " backward " or " uncivilized " or a " problem " that needs to be solved -- directly resulted in the creation of government-mandated residential schools , drastically interrupting our nations ' cultural and artistic development . For what artistic culture can thrive when its peoples ' children have been stolen from their arms ? When their community no longer has the medicine of children 's laughter to inspire them ? When their children come home unable to speak to them , their bodies covered with evidence of abuse they ca n't escape , their minds and spirits forever changed by abuse they dare not name ? While there are artists who emerged from the wreckage of these schools , I mourn the loss of the artists who may have been if they 'd had the support , and the Indigenous artistic movements that could have flourished if only Canada had n't marked our nations for destruction . <p> With the release of the TRC 's final report in 2015 , Canadians finally had to look at the effects of their country 's actions . The commission gave 94 calls to action that would help Indigenous and non-Indigenous people in Canada move toward reconciliation for these atrocities , and number 83 called on the Canada Council for the Arts " to establish , as a funding priority , a strategy for Indigenous and non-Indigenous artists to undertake collaborative projects and produce works that contribute to the reconciliation process . " The Canada Council for the Arts responded by creating the Reconciliation Initiative in 2015 , which funded collaborative arts projects between Indigenous and non-Indigenous artists and communities . They also announced in their 2016-2021 Strategic Plan that supporting Indigenous arts would be a key priority . <p> Many provincial arts councils have done the same : the arts councils in Ontario , British Columbia , Manitoba , Saskatchewan , New Brunswick , Nova Scotia and Quebec all made funding Indigenous arts one of their key priorities . What this means , in practical terms , is that arts organizations , publishers , literary journals and other arts institutions are not only encouraged to include Indigenous artists and our work but financially incentivized to do so . John Barton , former editor of The Malahat Review , described the impact this had in the afterword of the magazine 's first all-Indigenous issue , called " Indigenous Perspectives . " Barton wrote that the issue was " in part inspired by a letter the British Columbia Arts Council sent to literary magazines in 2015 , exhorting us not only to better represent Indigenous writers in our pages , but to involve them in our decision-making . " ( Basically , the B.C. government was telling the arts community they would n't get as much funding if they did n't try harder to include us . ) Instead of relying on non-Indigenous editors , Barton made the smart decision to invite Philip Kevin Paul , Richard Van Camp and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson to edit the issue . <p> This had a remarkable impact : once Indigenous artists were in charge of curating and editing Indigenous pieces -- once Indigenous art was allowed to be truly Indigenous -- the issue sold out completely and went into a second pressing . This is nearly unheard of in the literary world . It 's particularly impressive when you consider that , even five years ago , many non-Indigenous editors , tastemakers and gatekeepers in the literary community referred to Indigenous work as " niche , " claiming there was no audience for it . <p> To look at the contributors list of this issue now is a bit surreal . It included the first excerpt of Joshua Whitehead 's Jonny Appleseed . It included Lindsay Nixon 's essay " Windigo , " which eventually ended up in their book n ? t is ? nak . Billy-Ray Belcourt 's poem " Love is a Moontime Teaching " appeared here before it ended up in his Griffin Poetry Prize-winning book This Wound is a World . Darlene Naponse 's short story " She is Water " became a finalist for the 2017 Journey Prize after appearing in this issue . Darrel J. McLeod 's piece " Maci Manitowi ( Devils ) " was a precursor to his Governor General 's Literary Award-winning book Mamaskatch . My essay " A Mind Spread Out on the Ground " won a Gold medal at the National Magazine Awards that year , which helped me land an agent , and that piece eventually became the title essay of my essay collection . <p> This is the capitalistic reality behind all art : marginalized artists ' work will always be considered " niche " when arts institutions , publishers and galleries continue to treat it as niche . There will never be a large audience for marginalized art if arts institutions , publishers and galleries do n't financially back that art , exposing our work to Canadians on a large scale and thus creating an audience . And , of course , now that Indigenous artists have the chance to prove our work is both brilliant and marketable -- that we can sell out arts shows and end up on bestseller lists -- more arts institutions , publishers and galleries have supported us . It 's incredible how quickly these same institutions that shut us out changed their tunes and got on board once they realized we could not only get them awards recognition but also make them money . It 's also incredible how hungry Canadians have been for Indigenous art and stories once the government actually started to write us back into our collective history and institutions actually featured our work . <p> While the official politics of reconciliation has left much to be desired , with the government ultimately enacting few of the 94 calls to action , the cultural and artistic impact of the TRC 's final report can not be understated . It also shines its comedic light on gaps in communication that result from existing in a culture that often does n't understand the nuances of Asian family dynamics . One hilarious early example comes in the first-season episode " Rude Kid , " when the five-year-old son of Janet 's white professor is misbehaving and Appa ( Jung and Janet 's father , played by Paul Sun-Hyung Lee ) instinctively flicks the boy 's forehead -- and is quickly scolded for it . I was immediately taken back to moments when I was a child and my parents probably wanted to flick me on the head for doing something trivial in public ( Asian kid problems ) . <p> By showing something as little as a flick on the forehead , Kim 's Convenience has helped the rest of the world understand Asian family dynamics better . The show is a true accomplishment in Canadian television writing -- one that has not only shown that Canada is a mosaic of cultures , but that within these cultures , there are individual nuances that deserve time in the spotlight . " <p> When Everything , Everything was released on May 19 , 2017 , it made Canadian director Stella Meghie the only Black woman to have a wide release studio-backed feature film for the year . A lesser-known but perhaps even more important fact is that on this date , Meghie also became the first Black Canadian female filmmaker to ever have a wide release studio feature film . It 's a dubious honour on both accounts and points to the wide array of work that needs to be done not only in Hollywood but also here at home . The teen romance starring Amandla Stenberg and Nick Robinson was only Meghie 's second feature film , but it made Hollywood -- and the rest of the world -- sit up and pay attention to this visionary from the north as she broke barriers for Black Canadian female filmmakers . <p> Born in Toronto to Jamaican parents , Meghie always had a love for writing , but after graduating from Waterloo University , she could n't find a direct way into the industry and ended up working as a fashion publicist in New York . Ten years ago she made the decision that so many of us dream about : she quit her day job and decided to pursue her passion . When I spoke to Meghie about that decision on The Filmmakers in 2018 , she wisely noted , " It 's better to be scared than unhappy . " <p> After Meghie moved to London , England , and got her master 's degree in screenwriting , she wrote the first draft of what would become her debut feature film Jean of the Joneses . Five years later , after working as a production assistant , winning screenplay competitions , attending a summer crash course on directing , making a short film , attending writers retreats , several grants , getting consultations and receiving a fellowship , she finally premiered Jean of the Joneses at South by Southwest in 2016 -- to rave reviews . <p> The film follows a family dominated by Black women who are forced to confront secrets that have been hidden for decades when a man shows up at their door and promptly falls dead . There are few films in Hollywood and almost none in Canada that have a family of Black women at their centre ; as Meghie noted when I interviewed her , it 's a strange and unsettling privilege to be one of the first . " I wish I was adding to the canon instead of helping to create it . " <p> Jean of the Joneses was nominated for two Canadian Screen Awards ( including Best Original Screenplay ) and an Independent Spirit Award ( for Best First Screenplay ) . From there , Meghie 's journey becomes a bit of a filmmaker fairytale . She signed with Creative Artists Agency ( a.k.a . CAA a.k.a. one of the hottest Hollywood agencies to have in your corner ) , was approached by Warner Bros. and MGM to direct Everything , Everything and began booking gigs directing episodes of Insecure , Grown-ish and First Wives Club . In 2018 , her third feature film The Weekend premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival before being released in theatres earlier this year . And as 2019 comes to a close , social media is buzzing with excitement for her next film The Photograph , releasing Valentine 's Day 2020 and starring two of the biggest names in this current Black Hollywood Renaissance : Issa Rae and Lakeith Stanfield . <p> Although Meghie has been working on a wide variety of projects across film and television , they all share a common thread : messy , modern and creative Black female characters lead the narrative . She seems fascinated by the way these characters grow and change through their relationships , their passions , their career woes and their secrets . Happy to leave the big isms ( racism , sexism , classism ) and epic period pieces for other storytellers to tackle , Meghie 's interests are in the everyday lives of Black women today . Her stories explore intergenerational relationships and the way baggage and bad habits get passed down in families . She has a passion for romance and seems intrigued by the way it ignites vulnerability and inspires transformation . Her desire and determination to tell these stories is its own subversively political and transformative act : she 's taken the characters who , for decades , had been relegated to the best friend in the romantic comedy and readjusted the lens to focus on them . <p> It 's hard to be a filmmaker .
